title: Logistic growth and carrying capacity in a seal colony

stimulus.title: Gray seals on an island group after hunting stopped
stimulus.text: Hunting of gray seals on a group of islands stopped in 1960. Researchers counted the seals every 5 years from aerial photographs of the breeding beaches. Researchers estimate that r_max for this population is 0.12 per year.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the pattern of population growth from 1960 to 2020, and identify the approximate carrying capacity.

rubric.point: Describes slow growth at first, fastest growth in the middle years (about 1970-1985), then slowing and leveling off (S-shaped, logistic), with a carrying capacity of about 9,800-10,000 seals (accept any value from 9,700 to 10,000).
accept: increases quickly then levels off at about 9,900 seals
growth slows after about 1990 and the population stabilizes near 10,000

parts.sample: The population grew slowly at first, fastest between about 1970 and 1985, and then more and more slowly, leveling off from about 2005: an S-shaped, logistic curve. The carrying capacity is about 10,000 seals.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of population growth between 1975 and 1980, in seals per year.

accept: an increase of 300 seals each year on average

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use dN/dt = r_max N (K − N)/K, with r_max = 0.12 per year and K = 10,000, to calculate the growth rate when N = 9,000. Then explain why it is lower than the growth rate between 1975 and 1980, even though the population was larger.

rubric.point: Calculates 0.12 × 9,000 × (10,000 − 9,000)/10,000 = 108 seals per year, and explains that near K each seal has fewer resources (food, breeding space), so per capita births fall and/or deaths rise; the factor (K − N)/K is small.
accept: 108 per year; near carrying capacity competition for food and space lowers the per capita growth rate
about 110 seals per year, because only 10% of K is unused, so density-dependent factors slow growth
108; crowding reduces births and increases deaths, so each seal adds fewer offspring

parts.sample: dN/dt = 0.12 × 9,000 × (10,000 − 9,000)/10,000 = 0.12 × 9,000 × 0.1 = 108 seals per year. With 9,000 seals the colony is close to its carrying capacity, so there is little food and breeding space for each seal; intraspecific competition lowers births and raises deaths, so the per capita growth rate is small. In 1975-1980 the population was near K/2, where growth is fastest (300 per year).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: In 2020, a new fishery begins catching large numbers of the fish the seals eat. Predict the effect on the seal population over the next decade, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts that the seal population will decline (to a new, lower level), because less food lowers the carrying capacity, so the population is now above K and deaths exceed births (food is a density-dependent limiting resource).
accept: declines, because the carrying capacity falls when food is reduced
the population drops to a lower equilibrium since fewer fish can support fewer seals
decrease: N is now greater than the new K, so dN/dt becomes negative

parts.sample: The seal population will decline and level off at a lower number. Fish are the seals' limiting resource, so removing many fish lowers the carrying capacity. With N now above the new K, the factor (K − N)/K is negative: hungry seals have fewer pups and more die, until numbers fall to what the remaining fish can support.
